summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers Gamal Abdel Nasser's cultural legacy and his policies as Egyptian leader. It describes films about him, his social justice and economic nationalization programs in Egypt, his troubled Syrian union and the 1961 Syrian measures, and his handling of the Suez Canal nationalization and the 1956 tripartite invasion aftermath.
one_line: Overview of Gamal Abdel Nasser's film portrayals, domestic economic and social policies, the failed Syrian union, and the Suez Crisis.
key_facts: In 1963, Egyptian director Youssef Chahine produced the film El Nasser Salah El Dine ("Saladin The Victorious"), which drew parallels between Saladin and Gamal Abdel Nasser.
Ahmed Zaki played Gamal Abdel Nasser in Mohamed Fadel's 1996 film Nasser 56, which set the Egyptian box office record at the time.
The 1999 Syrian biopic Gamal Abdel Nasser was, together with the 1996 film Nasser 56, among the first biographical movies about contemporary public figures produced in the Arab world.
Gamal Abdel Nasser made Egypt fully independent of British influence, and the country became a major power in the developing world under his leadership.
Nasser considered establishing social justice a prerequisite to liberal democracy, one of his main domestic efforts.
On 8 February 1963, a military coup in Iraq led by a Ba'athist–Nasserist alliance toppled Qasim, who was subsequently shot dead.

A transitional unity agreement stipulating a federal system was signed on 17 April, with the new union set to be established in May 1965, but it fell apart weeks later when Syria's Ba'athists purged Nasser's supporters from the officers corps.
In July 1961, Nasser decreed socialist measures that nationalized wide-ranging sectors of the Syrian economy, which he attributed to control by the bourgeoisie.
In 1960, Nasser nationalized the Egyptian press to steer coverage towards socioeconomic issues and galvanize public support for his socialist measures.
Nasser believed the prospect of military intervention by France and the UK over the Suez Canal's nationalization was 80 per cent likely.
After an October UN Security Council resolution recognizing Egypt's right to control the canal, Heikal reported that Nasser estimated the danger of invasion had dropped to 10 per cent.
By the end of 1957, Nasser had nationalized all remaining British and French assets in Egypt, including the tobacco, cement, pharmaceutical, and phosphate industries.
Nasser initiated the Helwan steelworks, which subsequently became Egypt's largest enterprise.
Nasser decided to cooperate with the Soviet Union in constructing the Aswan Dam to replace the withdrawal of US funds.
Israel completed its withdrawal in March 1957 and released all Egyptian prisoners of war, while British and French forces totally withdrew by the end of December.
